transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do quick intros then jump into traffic and token mix. Uh, we have Devon and Riley from engineering.
[00:00:12] Laura (SpliceTech): Hi all, Laura here — Head of ML at SpliceTech. Tomás and Rajiv are on as well.
[00:00:18] Rajiv (SpliceTech): Yep, Rajiv, infra.
[00:00:22] Devon (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Quick note on recordings — this is being transcribed, may have small errors.
[00:00:30] Elena (SpliceTech): Thanks. We want to scope a POC to ensure Redwood meets our latency and cost targets before committing Dedicated capacity.
[00:00:38] Maya: Perfect. High level — today we'd like to collect the workload characteristics: QPS averages, burst patterns, concurrency, and token distributions (input vs output). Then align on the benchmark and success criteria.
[00:00:52] Laura: Sounds good. A little background: our main product is a conversational QA widget embedded in our dev docs portal. It handles multi-turn context, average history of 3 turns, sometimes long code snippets. Currently it's a mixture — some queries are short, some include 2–3k characters.
[00:01:10] Tomás (SRE): Traffic is mostly NA / EU, we see daily peaks around 11am PST and 6pm CET. Typical sustained QPS is between 18–35 and bursts up to 220 for a few minutes during product launches.
[00:01:29] Devon: Okay, that's helpful. When you say bursts to 220, is that global or region-specific?
[00:01:33] Tomás: That's global. Regionally, east coast and EU split roughly 60/40.
[00:01:38] Riley (Redwood): Do you have a concurrency measurement in terms of active requests per second vs inflight tokens?
[00:01:44] Laura: We have RPS metrics in our dashboard but not precise inflight token counts; we can pull token histograms. We do know average latency SLO target is 400ms p95 and 800ms p99 for interactive flows.
[00:01:56] Maya: Good to capture those. For the POC we'll need a representative sample of prompts — roughly 300–500 — that reflect the mix of short lookup queries vs long, context-heavy prompts. That helps us size KV cache hit-rate and prefix caching benefits.
[00:02:11] Elena: When you say KV cache, do you mean session KV or prefix caching? We use both — session state for conversation and prefixing for code blocks.
[00:02:19] Devon: Both patterns matter. Prefix caching reduces repeated token generation on similar prompts; session KV helps for long context reuse. For cost modeling we often present two scenarios: cache enabled (best-case) and cache disabled (conservative).
[00:02:34] Rajiv: Our concerns: data residency for some enterprise customers, and devs expect consistent latency. We're looking at both Hosted and Private.
[00:02:42] Maya: Noted. We'll include routing policies and a Private POC checklist if you want to try VPC peering.
[00:02:49] Tomás: Yes, we need to validate VPC peering and IP allowlist. Also KMS integration — we use HashiCorp Vault; KMS compatibility is required.
[00:02:58] Devon: Redwood supports KMS/HSM patterns; we'll note integration steps. For the workload: can you share percentile token lengths for input and output? median, p90, p99 would be ideal.
[00:03:09] Laura: We can get median input tokens ~40–60, output currently ranges more — median about 120 tokens, p90 around 900, p99 sometimes up to 2k when we return code examples.
[00:03:24] Maya: Great — that variance is important. For cost modeling we model token mix as a tri-modal distribution: short lookups (input 10–30 tokens, output 20–60), medium multi-turn (input 40–200, output 150–600), long code returns (input 200–800, output 800–2k).
[00:03:40] Laura: That aligns. What metrics do you typically run in the benchmark?
[00:03:44] Devon: We'll measure throughput/QPS until we hit latency SLOs, measure p50/p95/p99 latencies, token-throughput (tokens/sec), and cost per 1M generated tokens. We'll also run KV cache on/off to show delta. For concurrency we test varying client connection counts and sequence lengths.
[00:04:03] Elena: How long do benchmarks run? We worry about transient throttling affecting numbers.
[00:04:07] Riley: We usually do warmup, then multiple 10–15 minute sustained windows at target QPS. For burst behavior we run short 3–5 minute spiky tests. We'll also simulate cold-starts for models that need cold LLM weights loaded.
[00:04:21] Rajiv: Important: we need numbers for p99 latency at production-like token mixes, not just synthetic short prompts.
[00:04:26] Devon: Absolutely. That's why we ask for the sample corpus — we'll replay true token distributions and also create synthetic variations to fill edge cases.
[00:04:36] Maya: Let's talk success criteria. What would a pass look like for you?
[00:04:40] Laura: Two things: first, meet p95 < 400ms and p99 < 800ms for 90% of traffic mix; second, total cost per 1M tokens should be less than our current provider cost by at least 15% for comparable latency. Also, the platform must support our data residency and KMS needs.
[00:04:58] Maya: Clear. We'll map those to test cases. For the 90% traffic mix — do you want us to weight the medium multi-turn profile highest?
[00:05:06] Laura: Yes, about 70% medium multi-turn, 25% short lookups, 5% long code responses.
[00:05:13] Devon: Noted. For QPS/concurrency modeling: if sustained QPS is 25 and bursts 220, we need to know acceptable degradation patterns. Do you prefer graceful degradation with queued requests or failover to a cheaper model?
[00:05:26] Elena: Prefer graceful degradation — queue up to a short window (1–2s) then fallback to a smaller model for non-critical flows. Critical flows should have priority.
[00:05:35] Tomás: We'll want RBAC and per-route quotas to protect critical APIs.
[00:05:39] Maya: Redwood supports route-level SLOs and can route by policy. We'll show examples in the POC.
[00:05:44] Rajiv: About models — will you be testing open models or Redwood curated models?
[00:05:48] Devon: We recommend a 2-path bench: your preferred base model (open or privately licensed) and a lower-cost quantized variant. That shows cost/perf tradeoffs.
[00:05:58] Laura: Can you include a small hallucination QA check? We care about quality regressions after quantization.
[00:06:03] Riley: Yes — we'll add a lightweight eval harness: 50 gold prompts with expected answers; measure exact-match and semantic similarity. We'll include that in pass/fail criteria.
[00:06:14] Maya: Timeline — proposed: you share corpus and telemetry by 2025-12-23; Redwood prepares benchmark harness and schedules test slot 2025-12-26 to 2025-12-29; we deliver a POC report by 2026-01-06. Does that align?
[00:06:28] Laura: Tight but feasible. We have holidays the week of 12/22 but can prioritize export.
[00:06:33] Tomás: We can carve out an SRE window for tests on 12/27.
[00:06:37] Devon: We'll plan for a 2-hour deep benchmark plus 3 short burst windows.
[00:06:42] Elena: Final report — will that include cost modeling for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?
[00:06:48] Maya: We'll include cost per 1M tokens for Hosted and a rough Dedicated reserve estimate. Private/on-prem will have a separate checklist with infra assumptions.
[00:06:56] Rajiv: For Dedicated cost we need to know GPU types assumed and reserved sizing.
[00:07:01] Riley: We'll provide a recommended Dedicated footprint with GPUs, expected QPS per card, and cost amortization. We'll also show autoscale behavior.
[00:07:09] Laura: One last item: telemetry. We need guidance on what logs to capture during the benchmark.
[00:07:14] Devon: We'll ask for: per-request token counts, client-side latency, server-side latency (model and network split), cache hit rates, and error counts. A sample dashboard JSON will be shared.
[00:07:24] Maya: OK, let's surface risks: known risk is token spikes from code returns causing p99 blowups; second is KV cache miss patterns on first-time users.
[00:07:33] Rajiv: Also licensing for some large models — we might not be allowed to use a model in some jurisdictions.
[00:07:39] Devon: We'll include model-license notes; if needed we can test with a compatible smaller open model.
[00:07:45] Elena: How will you validate cold-starts? Our product sees idle periods with model unloading.
[00:07:50] Riley: We'll schedule cold-start scenarios by stopping the runtime and then initiating traffic, measuring load time and first-request latency. That will be separate from warm throughput tests.
[00:08:01] Laura: Great. Anything else?
[00:08:03] Maya: I want to confirm deliverables: editable QPS/concurrency spreadsheet, benchmark harness and runbook, POC report with latency/cost/quality, Dedicated sizing estimate, Private integration checklist.
[00:08:16] Laura: That covers it.
[00:08:18] Tomás: I'll coordinate VPC and KMS access with Rajiv.
[00:08:21] Rajiv: I'll confirm firewall rules and send a list of IPs.
[00:08:25] Devon: I'll draft the benchmark plan and post it to the shared folder.
[00:08:29] Maya: Okay — next immediate step: share the template worksheet, Laura shares sample prompts/telemetry. We'll reconvene after samples are uploaded.
[00:08:36] Elena: Thanks, everyone.
[00:08:38] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up in calendar.
[00:08:42] [End of recording — auto transcription may contain errors]
